issues.legal_issue: An acquisition made specifically for a private company, at its instance and for a site selected by it, is an acquisition for a company rather than a public-purpose acquisition where the asserted public scheme and qualifying public funding are not established.
material_facts: The company proposed a small-car project and identified the project site after discussions with the State.
Cabinet records and acquisition notifications connected the land to the company’s specific project.
The State-owned corporation raised the acquisition cost through loans; the State did not itself contribute the money, and the corporation was not a local authority for this purpose.
The procedures for acquisition for a company were not followed.
issues.conclusion: Justice V. Gopala Gowda held that the acquisition was for the company, not for a public purpose, and was invalid because the mandatory company-acquisition procedure was not followed. Justice Arun Mishra disagreed and held that it was a public-purpose acquisition; there was no common conclusion between the two opinions on this issue.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(f) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended in 1984, excludes acquisition for companies from public purpose; Sections 39–41 and Rules 3–5 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 govern acquisition for a company. Justice Gowda relied on Devender Singh v. State of Punjab, Royal Orchid Hotels Ltd. v. G. Jayaram Reddy, and the statutory scheme as explained in R.L. Arora. He distinguished pre-amendment authorities including Pandit Jhandu Lal, Somawanti, and Jage Ram, and considered Pratibha Nema distinguishable. Justice Mishra relied on Section 3(f), Section 6 and its Explanation 2, and the principle in Pratibha Nema that the source of acquisition funds is the principal distinction between the procedures; he also relied on Amarnath Ashram, Sooraram Pratap Reddy, Urmila Roy, and Nand Kishore Gupta.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.company_selected_project_site: A private company identified or selected the site used for the project for which the land was acquired.
predicates.acquisition_was_for_specific_company_pro: The acquisition records connected the land to a particular private company’s project.
predicates.acquisition_cost_not_paid_from_qualifyin: The acquisition cost was not paid from funds treated as public funds under the applicable acquisition scheme.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition challenge concerns land selected for a particular company’s project and the acquisition cost is not paid from qualifying public funds, the rule treats the acquisition as one for a company requiring the company-acquisition procedure.

issues.legal_issue: Land acquired by a State-owned corporation for an industrial project may be acquired for a public purpose under the ordinary acquisition procedure when the State adopts the project as part of its industrial policy and the corporation pays the acquisition cost.
material_facts: The State had an industrialization policy intended to attract investment, create employment, and develop the economy.
A State-owned corporation participated in the project from its inception, acquired the land, and paid the acquisition cost.
The land was leased to the private company for its project.
The project was expected to generate direct and indirect employment.
issues.conclusion: Justice Arun Mishra held that the acquisition was for a public purpose and that the ordinary acquisition procedure could be used; Justice V. Gopala Gowda disagreed. The opinions did not produce a common ruling on this issue.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(f)(iii) and (iv), and Section 6 including Explanation 2, of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, permit a public-purpose acquisition for a State-controlled corporation where the statutory conditions are met and expenditure by that corporation is treated as expenditure from public revenue. Justice Mishra relied on Somawanti, Jage Ram, Arnold Rodricks, Sooraram Pratap Reddy, Pratibha Nema, Urmila Roy, and Nand Kishore Gupta. He also applied the principle that a court should not substitute its view for the Government’s assessment of public purpose unless the acquisition is mala fide, collateral, irrational, or otherwise unlawful.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and state_owned_corporation_was_acquiring_body and state_adopted_industrial_policy and corporation_paid_acquisition_cost and project_expected_to_benefit_public

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.state_owned_corporation_was_acquiring_bo: A corporation owned or controlled by the State acquired the land.
predicates.state_adopted_industrial_policy: The State treated the project as part of a policy to promote industrial development.
predicates.corporation_paid_acquisition_cost: The State-owned corporation paid the cost of acquiring the land.
predicates.project_expected_to_benefit_public: The project was expected to create employment or otherwise benefit the public.

issues.definition: When a State-owned corporation acquires land under a State industrial policy, pays the acquisition cost, and undertakes a project expected to benefit the public, the rule permits the acquisition to proceed as a public-purpose acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A State may change its position in litigation about an earlier acquisition if the record supports the conclusion that the earlier action was unlawful, and the Supreme Court may examine the record rather than treating the parties’ affidavits as conclusive.
material_facts: The State’s position on the acquisition changed after a change of government.
The acquisition files, communications, Cabinet records, and statutory notifications were before the Court.
The Court was asked to reject the State’s changed position because of its earlier pleadings.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the objection to the State’s changed position and examined the underlying record to determine whether the acquisition was lawful.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers a wide discretionary jurisdiction to address injustice. A State may not change its position merely for political reasons, but may do so where the earlier action is shown to be contrary to law or public policy. The Court relied on Andhra Pradesh Dairy Development Corpn. Federation v. B. Narasimha Reddy, M.I. Builders Pvt. Ltd. v. Radhey Shyam Sahu, and P.S.R. Sadanatham v. Arunachalam.

predicates.supreme_court_appellate_proceeding: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appellate or special-leave proceeding.
predicates.state_changed_its_litigation_position: The State took a position in the proceeding different from its earlier position.
predicates.record_shows_earlier_state_action_may_be: Documents and other material in the record provide a basis to question the legality of the earlier State action.

issues.definition: When the State changes its position in a Supreme Court proceeding and the record raises a legal concern about its earlier action, the rule allows the Court to examine that record despite the State’s earlier position.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory opportunity to object to a proposed acquisition is a substantive safeguard requiring a genuine hearing, objective consideration of objections, and an independent governmental decision before a final declaration.
material_facts: The Cabinet had already decided to acquire the particular land before the preliminary notification and inquiry.
Landowners and cultivators filed objections, including objections concerning existing uses and livelihoods.
Some objectors were not afforded an effective opportunity to be heard, and the Collector rejected objections without adequately addressing them.
The State mechanically accepted the Collector’s report without independently considering the objections.
The proposed project was later abandoned.
issues.conclusion: Both opinions found the inquiry and consideration of objections defective and agreed that the acquisition proceedings were vitiated; the Supreme Court quashed the acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5-A(2) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require the Collector to hear objectors and objectively report on their objections, and require the Government to consider that report and make its own decision before declaring the land needed. The Court relied on Raghubir Singh Sherawat v. State of Haryana, Surinder Singh Brar v. Union of India, Kamal Trading (P) Ltd. v. State of West Bengal, Usha Stud & Agricultural Farms (P) Ltd. v. State of Haryana, Gojer Brothers Private Ltd. v. State of West Bengal, and related decisions. Justice Arun Mishra explained that individual notices are not required for the Section 5-A inquiry if the prescribed public notifications are made, but that the hearing and consideration must be genuine and objective.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and objections_were_filed and acquisition_decision_preceded_effective_objection_review and objections_not_objectively_considered

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.objections_were_filed: People with interests in the land submitted objections to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_decision_preceded_effective_: The decision to acquire the particular land was made before the statutory objection process could operate meaningfully.
predicates.objections_not_objectively_considered: The Collector or Government failed to give the objections genuine consideration or the Government merely endorsed the Collector’s report.

issues.definition: When objections are filed but the decision to acquire the particular land precedes meaningful review and the objections are not objectively considered, the rule treats the acquisition proceedings as invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An award made after a collective inquiry without the required individual notices and fair opportunity to establish compensation claims is legally defective, although the opinions differed on its effect on the acquisition itself.
material_facts: The Collector did not serve individual notices on the landowners and cultivators for the compensation inquiry.
A joint inquiry was conducted and compensation was determined by combining multiple matters into composite awards.
The affected people were not given an adequate opportunity to establish their claims about the land’s market value.
Supplementary or consent awards were also made.
issues.conclusion: Justice V. Gopala Gowda held that the composite awards were invalid for failure to conduct the required inquiry and determine compensation lawfully. Justice Arun Mishra held that failure to serve the individual notices required for compensation invalidated the awards and required fresh determination, but did not invalidate the notifications; he also held that a challenge to compensation adequacy should be pursued by a statutory reference. The opinions differed on the scope of the defect, and the acquisition was quashed on the separate, common ground of the defective objection process.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 9 and 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require notice and a proper inquiry into claims and compensation. Justice Gowda treated the Collector’s compensation determination as a quasi-judicial exercise requiring individual consideration and relied on the statutory requirements and natural justice. Justice Mishra relied on Sections 9(1), 9(3), 11, and 18, holding that personal service under Section 9(3) is mandatory, while inadequacy of compensation is addressed through a reference under Section 18.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition or an award made in that acquisition.
predicates.compensation_inquiry_was_joint: The compensation claims for multiple land interests were dealt with through a collective inquiry or composite award.
predicates.individual_claimants_lacked_required_not: Individual claimants were not given the notice or opportunity needed to present their compensation claims.

issues.definition: When a collective compensation inquiry denies individual claimants the required notice or a fair opportunity to present their claims, the rule treats the resulting award as invalid.

issues.legal_issue: Where an acquisition is invalid and the project has been abandoned, the land may be restored to its former owners or occupiers without requiring repayment of compensation already received.
material_facts: The acquisition proceedings were held invalid because the statutory objection process had not been properly followed.
The private company abandoned the project, removed its machinery, and relocated the project elsewhere.
The land had been taken from its owners and cultivators and its condition had changed during the period of possession.
The owners and cultivators had been deprived of the use of their land for an extended period.
issues.conclusion: The Court quashed the acquisition and directed restoration of the land to the respective landowners and cultivators. Compensation already paid was not to be recovered, and persons who had not withdrawn compensation could withdraw it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its remedial powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice. It concluded that, because the project had failed and the acquisition was invalid, remitting the matter for a new objection inquiry would be futile. Both opinions agreed on restoration and retention of compensation, while Justice Arun Mishra also referred to the compensation principles in Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Virupax Shankar Nadagouda and Collector, Land Acquisition v. Gana Ram Dhoba.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and acquisition_proceedings_are_invalid and project_was_abandoned and landowners_were_deprived_of_land_use

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_proceedings_are_invalid: The acquisition has been held invalid for a legal defect.
predicates.project_was_abandoned: The project for which the land was acquired was discontinued or relocated.
predicates.landowners_were_deprived_of_land_use: The owners or cultivators lost possession or use of their land because of the acquisition.

issues.definition: When an invalid acquisition was made for a project that has been abandoned after depriving owners of their land, the rule provides for restoration without recovery of compensation already paid.
